Cost Guides

House Extension Cost in Toronto 2026

A complete 2026 breakdown of what a house extension costs in Toronto — by addition type, by square footage, and by what actually moves the price.

Updated for 2026 · 8 min read

Book Consultation

  • What Are Typical Costs?
  • Why Do Costs Vary?
  • Cost Breakdown by Addition Type

If you're planning a house extension in Toronto — expanding the kitchen, adding a second storey, or building out to fit a growing family — this guide walks through what it costs, why costs vary, how to budget, and how to maximize value. It's built around the City of Toronto market specifically.

What Are Typical Costs?

Here are current ballparks for home extensions in Toronto (2026), based on recent industry sources:

  • Basic home additions (standard finishes, less complexity): CAD $380–$400 per sq ft.
  • Mid-range additions (upgraded materials, some complexity): $450–$500 per sq ft.
  • High-end or complex additions (luxury finishes, structural modifications, custom design): can exceed $650+ per sq ft.

To give an example, many full home additions in Toronto are quoted between $420,000 and $820,000 including taxes for a typical project size. If you're adding roughly 400 sq ft of space with standard finishes, you're looking at somewhere around $140,000–$160,000 (400 × $350–$400 per sq ft). For higher-end finishes, the same footprint can run $220,000+.

Why Do Costs Vary? Key Cost Factors

Several variables influence the final cost of a house extension in Toronto. Knowing them helps with realistic budgeting and cost-effective choices.

Size & Scope

  • Larger additions benefit from some economy of scale (cost per sq ft can drop slightly), but total cost is higher.
  • A simple single-room extension differs greatly from a full second storey or a complex integration with the existing house.

Type of Addition & Structural Requirements

  • A ground-floor room versus a second storey: a second storey often requires reinforcing foundations, structural modifications, and staircases, which adds cost.
  • Foundations, piles, or slab work vary in cost — additions built on a full foundation/slab can cost more than those on piles because of excavation and insulation implications.

Materials & Finishes

  • Standard materials (drywall, standard windows, good-but-not-premium finishes) sit at the lower end of the range.
  • High-end materials (custom cabinetry, stone, high-performance windows, luxury flooring) push costs up significantly.

Labour, Contractor & Location Specifics

  • Toronto's labour market and site constraints (tight lots, older homes, limited access) can increase costs.
  • Contractor experience, scheduling, and seasonal demand also affect price.

Permits, Professional Fees & Regulations

  • Permits and code compliance matter — in Toronto you must account for zoning, bylaw setbacks, heritage overlays (if any), and building permits.
  • Architectural and engineering fees are often a meaningful share of the total budget.
  • Unexpected structural issues (hidden damage, soil issues) often raise costs, so a contingency is recommended.

Site Conditions & Access

Older homes, difficult access, limited staging space, close neighbours, and excavation for a basement or second storey all add cost.

Cost Breakdown by Addition Type

Rear Addition

A rear addition extends your home's footprint into the backyard. It's the most common type in Toronto and typically involves a new foundation, framing, a roofline tie-in, and full interior finishing, including plumbing and electrical if a kitchen or bathroom is included.

Typical cost: $150,000 to $300,000

What drives cost up: adding a bathroom or kitchen, complex roofline tie-ins, excavation on a tight urban lot, and matching existing finishes throughout.

What drives cost down: a simple rectangular footprint, a slab or post foundation instead of full excavation, and standard finishes.

Second Storey Addition

Adding a full second floor to a bungalow is a major structural project. The existing roof is removed, first-floor walls are reinforced or rebuilt, and an entirely new floor is framed, insulated, and finished. In North York, Leaside, and Lawrence Park, this is one of the most common projects on post-war bungalow streets.

Typical cost: $300,000 to $500,000+

A second storey effectively doubles your living space without reducing your yard. It's the highest-cost addition type but also the one with the most significant impact on property value and livability.

What drives cost up: extensive structural reinforcement of existing walls, HVAC upgrades, staircase integration, and high-end finishes throughout.

What drives cost down: simpler roof design, standard finishes, and a structurally sound existing first floor that doesn't require a full rebuild.

Bump-Out

A bump-out extends one room — typically a kitchen, dining area, or bedroom — by 2 to 8 feet. It's far less disruptive than a full addition because it often doesn't require full foundation excavation; a cantilevered or post-supported structure is sometimes sufficient.

Typical cost: $60,000 to $150,000

Best for homeowners who need targeted space in one area rather than a full addition.

In-Law Suite or Multi-Generational Addition

A self-contained unit with its own entrance, kitchen, and bathroom, either attached to the main home or built as a garden or laneway suite. In the GTA, where multi-generational living is common, this addition type consistently delivers strong ROI and rental income potential.

Typical cost: $175,000 to $350,000

Zoning and servicing requirements vary by lot and neighbourhood — always verify with the City of Toronto before committing to a design.

What's Included in the Cost

Every home addition in Toronto involves several cost layers beyond the construction itself.

  • Permits and approvals: All home additions require a building permit from the City of Toronto, no exceptions. Budget $3,000 to $10,000+ depending on project size and whether a Committee of Adjustment variance is required.
  • Architectural drawings: A licensed architect or designer must stamp drawings for permit submission. Expect $8,000 to $20,000 for a full set of architectural and structural drawings.
  • Structural engineering: Second storey additions and any load-bearing changes require a structural engineer. Budget $3,000 to $8,000 for engineering drawings and site reviews.
  • HVAC and mechanical: Extending your home's footprint means extending or upgrading your heating, cooling, and ventilation systems. This is one of the most commonly underestimated costs, particularly in older Toronto homes.
  • Site logistics: Urban Toronto lots are tight. Crane costs, traffic management, waste removal, and temporary weather protection can add $10,000 to $30,000 on a complex project.

One-Storey vs. Second-Storey Additions

Since one-storey additions come up often, it's worth comparing them to building upward.

  • A one-storey addition typically does not require full foundation reinforcement (unless the existing foundation is weak), compared with adding a second storey — this can reduce complexity, disruption, and cost.
  • However, you are investing in a new roof, exterior walls, possibly new mechanical systems, and a full foundation or slab depending on design.
  • According to industry sources, second-storey additions in Toronto cost approximately $312–$390 CAD/sq ft (unfinished) or $360–$432 CAD/sq ft (turnkey).
  • In many cases, a one-storey addition can cost somewhat less per square foot than a full second-storey build, but the actual cost depends heavily on site conditions and finishes.

Budgeting Tips & Contingency Planning

Given the variability, here are some practical budgeting considerations:

  • Set aside contingency: 15–20% of your budget is wise for unforeseen conditions.
  • Obtain multiple quotes: Compare not just price but scope, materials, and timelines.
  • Define finish level early: Materials and finishes make a big difference, so decide early.
  • Confirm permits and zoning early: Unexpected delays or requirement changes add cost.
  • Break the project into distinct phases: Demolition and structural work first, finishes later.
  • Consider living arrangements during construction: Major work may require alternate accommodation, which adds cost.
  • Evaluate return on investment: Extensions add space and value, but cost should align with the expected value increase in your neighbourhood.
  • Stick to your scope: Change orders during construction are a common cost driver.

Return on Investment & Value Impact

  • Extensions in Toronto not only increase livable space but can boost resale value, especially in tight-lot older neighbourhoods where moving is difficult.
  • ROI depends on neighbourhood, market conditions, quality of finish, and how seamlessly the addition integrates with the existing home.
  • Overbuilding (in finish level or size) relative to neighbourhood norms may not always see full cost recovery.

Special Considerations for Toronto Homeowners

  • Many Toronto homes have limited lot coverage or narrow side yards — zoning and bylaw requirements (setbacks, lot coverage, height limits) may restrict what you can do.
  • Older homes may require structural upgrades (foundation, crawlspace, roof) when you attach an extension, which can add cost.
  • Infrastructure: electrical, HVAC, and plumbing may need upgrading if you expand significantly.
  • Heritage or conservation zones: additional restrictions and costs may apply.
  • Seasonal and contractor availability: Toronto's busy construction market can mean longer lead times or higher labour costs.

Summary & Takeaways

  • Average cost per sq. ft. for a house extension in Toronto in 2026: $380–$560 for standard to mid-range work; high-end custom projects now typically exceed $650+.
  • A full addition (hundreds of square feet) often costs $230,000–$650,000+, depending on size, complexity, and 2026 market rates for specialized trades.
  • Major cost drivers: Size and scope, structural requirements, material and finish level, labour and site conditions, and updated 2026 municipal permit and development fees.
  • Set a realistic budget: Include a 15%–20% contingency (up from 10% in previous years) to account for 2026 supply-chain shifts. Engage experienced professionals early (architect, engineer, contractor), define finish levels clearly, and verify the 2026 zoning and permit path, especially regarding new "Missing Middle" and "Net-Zero" guidelines.
  • The bottom line: With good planning, an extension remains one of the most effective ways to increase both living space and property value in Toronto — especially as the 2026 real estate market makes the cost of selling and upsizing increasingly prohibitive.
